title: Athletics: javelin throw
rulebook: World Athletics Competition and Technical Rules 2024: TR 32.9 (the javelin runway and its arc), TR 32.12 (the sector), TR 32.14, 32.16, 32.17 and 32.20 (throwing events: failures, the landing, leaving the runway, the measurement), TR 38.1 (the throw), TR 38.3-38.6 (the javelin: the women's implement, its grip)
deviations: TR 38.1(a) ("the javelin shall be held at the grip with one hand"): the hand is the H1-2's own Inspire five-finger hand (six drives: four fingers, the thumb's flexion and rotation; fingertip forces 20 N, the thumb 30 N, at 1.0 times these forces; one closure command for the whole hand); the cord lies across its palm and is held by its fingers' and thumb's contact and friction only. Held means the cord touching the hand's fingers and its thumb or palm; the hold may break for at most 0.02 s (contacts flicker); the release is the javelin's last contact with any part of you once the hold has ended, when it has then touched nothing of you for 0.02 s (between the end of the hold and the release only the right arm may touch it, for at most 0.2 s). "Over the shoulder or upper part of the throwing arm" is judged at the release: the javelin's centre of gravity must then be at least 0.0 m higher than the throwing shoulder's joint.
TR 38.1(a) (one hand): before the release the javelin may not touch your left arm or hand (it may rest against the rest of you: the rule book forbids only the second hand).
TR 38.1(c): "turned completely around" is judged as the chest's heading more than 135.0 degrees away from the throwing direction at any time before the release.

TR 38.3-38.6 (the implement): the robot throws the women's javelin, 600 g and 2.21 m (the men's is 800 g and 2.60-2.70 m): the H1-2's swing, holding the javelin by friction alone, cannot release the men's javelin pointing along its path fast enough to throw it head first past a line (its best: 15.3 m); a lighter official implement leaves faster from the same arm. Everything about the throw is otherwise real.

TR 38.3-38.6: the javelin is one rigid body (no bending or vibration) whose head does not stick in the ground; the mark is the point where the head first touches the ground; the cord grip is a smooth band 0.145 m long and 0.0287 m across (no pattern: the finger pads' rubber gives the friction).

Flight: quasi-steady aerodynamics in still air, no wind: drag and lift against the angle of attack from the wind-tunnel measurement of this very kind of javelin (a World Athletics women's javelin, Seo et al., Scientific Reports 2023; drag, lift and pitching moment from 0 to 18 degrees, beyond that a cylinder's cross-flow); the shaft's cross-flow damps its rotation. The javelin does not bend or vibrate.
TR 32.15 (interrupting a trial, laying the implement down): not modelled; the first release is the throw, and the javelin may not be gripped again.

TR 38.1(a) ("held at the grip with one hand ... shall not be slung or hurled"): the throw is the hand's alone and its release clean. The rule book has no article on touching the javelin after it has left the hand; here the right arm may still brush it during 0.2 s after the release, but those touches may change its velocity by at most 0.5 m/s in all (the sum of their contact impulses over its mass): a harder touch is a second propulsion of a released implement, and fails the throw.
TR 32.14 names no fall: here a fall ends the trial as a failure, as in every task of this benchmark; the trial ends when the robot has left the runway correctly and stands.
TR 25.17 (one minute for a trial): the whole trial, leaving the runway included, has 60 s.
The qualifying mark of 20.0 m is this benchmark's (a girls' school standard for the 600 g javelin); the rule book only measures.

texts.sentence: Throw the javelin held by its cord in your right hand over the shoulder from behind the arc so that its head strikes the ground first, inside the sector, at least 20.0 m from the arc, then leave the runway behind the arc and stand.
texts.rules: The women's javelin (0.6 kg, 2.21 m long, its centre of gravity 0.92 m from the tip, a metal head of 0.28 m; its cord grip, 0.145 m long and 0.0287 m across, covers the centre of gravity) starts held at its cord across the palm of your right hand, a five-finger hand that holds only by contact and friction: the javelin can slip along the fingers or turn in the hand, and drop. It is held while the cord touches the hand's fingers and its thumb or palm (breaks of at most 0.02 s are ignored). The release is the javelin's last contact with any part of you after the hold has ended (however it ends: opened, slipped or dropped), once it has then touched nothing of you for 0.02 s; between the end of the hold and the release only your right arm and hand may touch it, for at most 0.2 s. Until the release the javelin may not touch your left arm or hand (the javelin is held with one hand). The runway is 4.0 m wide between the inner edges of its side lines and 30.0 m long; it ends at the arc, a white strip whose inner edge is a circle of 8.0 m radius round a point on the runway's centre line; short white lines run outwards from the arc's two ends at right angles to the side lines. The sector is bounded by the two lines from the arc's centre through the arc's ends (28.96 degrees between them). The throw: at the release the javelin's centre of gravity must be at least 0.0 m higher than your right shoulder joint. There is one release: after it the javelin may not be held again (the cord in the hand's fingers and thumb or palm once more) and no part of you may touch it, except that your right arm and its hand may still brush it during the first 0.2 s, if those touches change its velocity by at most 0.5 m/s in all (the sum of their contact impulses over its mass: the release must be clean). The throw is valid only if the head touches the ground before any other part of the javelin, at a point inside the sector lines (on a line is out). It is measured from that point to the inner edge of the arc along the line through the arc's centre. You succeed when a valid throw measures at least 20.0 m and you have then left the runway correctly and stood for 1.0 s. Leaving correctly: after the javelin has landed, your first touch of a side line or of the ground outside the runway is behind the arc's end lines, or you touch the ground 4.0 m or more behind the arc's ends. Standing: only your feet on the ground, the torso within about 20 degrees of upright, the pelvis slower than 0.35 m/s. You fail if, at any time before that, any part of you touches the arc, its end lines or the ground beyond them; if you touch a side line or the ground outside the runway (also behind its rear end) before the javelin has landed; if your chest is turned more than 135.0 degrees away from the throwing direction before the release (your back to the arc); if the javelin touches your left arm or hand before the release; if it is released lower than the shoulder; if after the end of the hold it stays on your right arm for more than 0.2 s or touches another part of you; if it is held again, or touched, after the release (but for the brush above); if it does not land head first, lands outside the sector or short of 20.0 m; if you fall (your pelvis lower than 0.5 m above the ground, or any part of you other than your feet on the ground); or after 60 s. Where you touch the ground is judged on the points of contact.
texts.venue: You stand on the runway's centre line facing the sector (+x), your pelvis 2.0 m behind the middle of the arc; the arc's centre is 6.0 m behind you, its ends are 0.25 m behind its middle and 2.0 m to either side, and the runway reaches 28 m behind you. Your right arm hangs down, the hand's fingers pointing down; the javelin lies level across the closed hand's palm, its cord held by the fingers and thumb, pointing forwards (the tip 0.92 m ahead of the hand). Still air. The hand opens when your right grip command goes to 0 (the fingers at most 260 deg/s).
texts.difficulty: 20.0 m asks for a release near 18 m/s at 25 to 30 degrees with the javelin pointing close enough to its flight that it comes down head first; the H1-2 has no running policy and its arm motors give 40 N m at the shoulder. Nothing holds the 2.21 m javelin but the fingers round its cord: a whip of the arm pulls it out across them (the finger drives give way at their self-locking limits), and the hand must let go of it at the right moment, above the shoulder, on a body that has to stay on its feet behind the arc.

stand.meaning: the platform holds the legs in the stance; you give the waist's 1 and the arms' 14 joint targets (rad) (grip_right: the right hand's closure command, 0 (open, the fingers straight) to 1 (every drive closing towards its closed position; fingers stop on what they touch))

walk.meaning: Unitree's walking policy drives the legs from the velocity command (vx forward, vy to the left, m/s; wz turning left, rad/s; the robot's own frame); you give the waist and arm joint targets (grip_right: the right hand's closure command, 0 (open, the fingers straight) to 1 (every drive closing towards its closed position; fingers stop on what they touch))

joints.meaning: you give all 27 joint targets (rad); the default PD gains, no feed-forward (grip_right: the right hand's closure command, 0 (open, the fingers straight) to 1 (every drive closing towards its closed position; fingers stop on what they touch))

lowcmd.meaning: Unitree's LowCmd for all 27 joints: position targets (rad), velocity targets (rad/s), feed-forward torques (N m), kp, kd; the motor torque is kp (q - q_measured) + kd (dq - dq_measured) + tau, evaluated at 1 kHz (grip_right: the right hand's closure command, 0 (open, the fingers straight) to 1 (every drive closing towards its closed position; fingers stop on what they touch))

robot.name: unitree_h1
robot.title: Unitree H1-2
robot.model: Unitree H1-2, 27 joints, 1.78 m, 67 kg (RoboOlympics robot library h1-4: the H1-2 body (Unitree's own h1_2 model, its joint ranges and speed limits) with Unitree H2 / H2-X-class leg actuators from the H2's official URDF (hips and knees 360 N m, ankle pitch 66.88 N m; curves of Unitree's M107 shape, 2.5 kW peak per joint) and H2-class arm actuators from the same URDF (shoulder pitch 130 N m; shoulder roll and yaw, elbow, forearm roll 60 N m; curves of Unitree's N7520 / N5020 shapes); the H1-2's own torso (M107-15, 200 N m), ankle roll and wrist pitch / yaw (estimates))

grip.rule: a closed grip holds the nearest grippable object whose surface is within reach_m of the palm (a point 4.5 cm beyond the wrist flange along the forearm) and that moves no faster than max_relative_speed_m_s relative to it; opening the grip lets it go

right.model: the H1-2's Inspire RH56DFX five-finger hand (6 self-locking linear drives for 12 joints: the thumb's rotation and flexion, one drive per finger with its two joints coupled; Unitree's H1-2 kinematics) with H2-class fingertip forces: 20 N per finger and 30 N the thumb, 2 x the RH56DFX's 10 / 15 N (Unitree's H2 Plus offers 20 N Sharpa Wave hands; Inspire's RH56E2 gives 28 / 30 N)

servo.rule: each drive: a setpoint moves towards open + closure x (closed - open) at most speed_rad_s, but closing stops where kp (setpoint - q) would exceed active_torque_nm; torque = clip(kp (setpoint - q) + kd (setpoint speed - dq), -passive, passive) at every physics step; a load beyond passive_torque_nm drags the setpoint (the drive slips)

right.holding_rule: a free body that touches the hand's fingers and its thumb or palm
